review_note: Pinned derived.tex 12387–12398 asserts for a countable inverse system in triangulated D, its pro-object is essentially constant precisely if after some index every A_j decomposes as A⊕Z_j with transition maps identity on fixed A and the Z-system prozero. The two decomposition compatibility conditions and existential quantifiers are preserved in Stage A.
statement:
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a triangulated category. Let $(A_i)$ be an inverse system
in $\mathcal{D}$. Then $(A_i)$ is essentially constant (see
Categories, Definition
\ref{categories-definition-essentially-constant-diagram})
if and only if there exists an $i$ and for all $j \geq i$ a direct sum
decomposition $A_j = A \oplus Z_j$ such that
(a) the maps $A_{j'} \to A_j$ are compatible with the direct sum
decompositions and identity on $A$, (b) for all $j \geq i$ there exists some
$j' \geq j$ such that $Z_{j'} \to Z_j$ is zero.

review_note: Source 12415–12440: in an inverse system of distinguished triangles A_n→B_n→C_n→A_n[1], essential constancy of both endpoints forces middle B_n essentially constant, and the values A,B,C form distinguished triangle with compatible comparison maps from some stage. The draft retains both endpoint assumptions and the triangle/compatibility conclusion; no claim of all stages being constant.
statement:
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a triangulated category. Let
$$
A_n \to B_n \to C_n \to A_n[1]
$$
be an inverse system of distinguished triangles in $\mathcal{D}$.
If $(A_n)$ and $(C_n)$ are essentially constant, then
$(B_n)$ is essentially constant and their values fit into
a distinguished triangle $A \to B \to C \to A[1]$ such that for
some $n \geq 1$ there is a map
$$
\xymatrix{
A_n \ar[d] \ar[r] &
B_n \ar[d] \ar[r] &
C_n \ar[d] \ar[r] &
A_n[1] \ar[d] \\
A \ar[r] &
B \ar[r] &
C \ar[r] &
A[1]
}
$$
of distinguished triangles which induces an isomorphism
$\lim_{n' \geq n} A_{n'} \to A$ and similarly for $B$ and $C$.

review_note: Pinned 12489–12502 requires a UNIFORM finite amplitude interval [a,b] for all A_n, and every cohomology pro-system H^i(A_n) essentially constant. It yields essential constancy in D(A) and the value's cohomologies equal the pro-system values. Stage A keeps uniform bound and all integers i.
statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an abelian category. Let $A_n$ be an inverse
system of objects of $D(\mathcal{A})$. Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exist integers $a \leq b$ such that $H^i(A_n) = 0$
for $i \not \in [a, b]$, and
\item the inverse systems $H^i(A_n)$ of $\mathcal{A}$ are essentially constant
for all $i \in \mathbf{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $A_n$ is an essentially constant system of $D(\mathcal{A})$ whose
value $A$ satisfies that $H^i(A)$ is the value of the constant system
$H^i(A_n)$ for each $i \in \mathbf{Z}$.

review_note: Source 12520–12530: if an inverse system of distinguished triangles has a cone system C_n that is PRO-ZERO (essentially constant with value zero), then maps A_n→B_n give an ISOMORPHISM in pro-D, not necessarily individual A_n→B_n isomorphisms. Stage A retains this vital pro-qualification.
statement:
Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a triangulated category. Let
$$
A_n \to B_n \to C_n \to A_n[1]
$$
be an inverse system of distinguished triangles. If the system $C_n$
is pro-zero (essentially constant with value $0$), then the maps
$A_n \to B_n$ determine a pro-isomorphism between the pro-object $(A_n)$
and the pro-object $(B_n)$.

review_note: Source 12549–12566: if the maps A_n→B_n of D(A) have a COMMON uniform bounded cohomological interval and yield pro-isomorphisms on cohomology in EVERY degree, then they yield a pro-isomorphism in D(A). Stage A preserves both finite amplitude and all-degree hypotheses.
statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an abelian category.
$$
A_n \to B_n
$$
be an inverse system of maps of $D(\mathcal{A})$. Assume
\begin{enumerate}
\item there exist integers $a \leq b$ such that $H^i(A_n) = 0$
and $H^i(B_n) = 0$ for $i \not \in [a, b]$, and
\item the inverse system of maps $H^i(A_n) \to H^i(B_n)$ of $\mathcal{A}$
define an isomorphism of pro-objects of $\mathcal{A}$
for all $i \in \mathbf{Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the maps $A_n \to B_n$
determine a pro-isomorphism between the pro-object $(A_n)$
and the pro-object $(B_n)$.
